# Concentration of rare earth elements during high temperature pyrolysis of waste printed circuit boards

c Facultad de Ingenieria, Universidad Andres Bello. Antonio Varas 880, Providencia, Santiago, Chile

## ABSTRACT

An in-depth investigation was carried out on the recovery of rare earth elements (REEs) from a variety of waste printed circuit boards (PCBs). High temperature pyrolysis was carried out at 850 C for 15 min using horizontal resistance and thermal plasma furnaces with different levels of turbulence. The concentration of REEs in key pyrolysis residues, namely, copper rich red metallic fraction, lead/tin rich white metallic fraction and slag rich carbonaceous residues, were determined using ICP analysis. Most of the REEs were found concentrated in the carbonaceous residue with negligible levels of REEs recovered in the two metallic fractions. Most of the recovered REEs showed a high affinity towards to refractory oxides silica and alumina, and little affinity towards metals Cu, Pb and Sn. The yield of REEs was significantly higher from the plasma furnace indicating the important role of turbulence in the dissociation & subsequent diffusion of REEs during pyrolysis. While La, Pr, Sm and Y required turbulent conditions for their recovery, Nd, Gd, Ce and Dy were relatively easy to dissociate and extract from the waste. Significant amounts of REEs could thus be recovered from waste PCBs as concentrated recyclates for further processing and extraction of individual rare earths. This study has shown that PCBs could prove to be a valuable urban mining resource of REEs. The recovery of REEs, in addition to precious and other metals, could play an important role towards enhancing the economic and environmental sustainability of e-waste recycling.

## 1. Introduction

Rare earth elements (REEs) are playing an increasingly crucial and vital role in the electronics industry in applications such as Plasma screens, LEDs, Cathode-ray tubes (CRTs), permanent NdFeB magnets, mobile phones, computers and peripherals, motors, wind turbines, rechargeable batteries etc. (Binnemans et al., 2013). Several REEs, such as Neodymium (Nd), Praseodymium (Pr), Gadolinium (Gd), Dysprosium (Dy), Terbium (Tb), Lanthanum (La), Cerium (Ce), Europium (Eu), Terbium (Tb), Yttrium (Y), are essential to the manufacture of several electronic components. These components include permanent magnets (Nd, Pr, Gd, Dy and Tb); rechargeable batteries (La, Ce, Nd and Pr), phosphors (Eu, Tb, Y, Ce, Gd, La), plasma screens (Eu, Tb, Y, Ce, La), auto catalysts (Dy, Nd, Pr, Tb) and other applications (Curtis, 2010). Due to increasing demand, high prices, restricted supplies and monopoly issues, U.S. Department of Energy (2011) has identified five REEs, i.e., Nd, Eu,

Tb, Dy and Y, as most critical resources in terms of medium-term criticality index. Over the next 25 years, the demand for Nd and Dy is expected to rise by 700% and 2600% respectively for applications in green, low-carbon economies and other potential sectors (Alonso et al., 2012).

Rare earth elements are not exactly rare in nature; these can be found in more than 200 minerals (British Geological Survey, 2011). However, key difficulties in their mining are caused by low concentrations in poor grade ores for economic and sustainable mining, the production of radioactive thorium as a biproduct, regulatory pressures etc. (Kara et al., 2010). With China presently supplying over 90% of the market share of REEs, creating a near monopoly situation, the availability of REEs to enterprises outside China can be potentially challenging, limited by export quotas, expensive, crucial and even a political issue (Moss et al., 2013; Hoenderdaal et al., 2013). Other countries that produce REEs include Australia, USA, India, Brazil, Malaysia etc. In view of emerging new technologies based on REEs and the present supply situation, efforts are being made for further exploration, mining, and enhancing process efficiency of various process steps. Recycling of REEs (presently < 1%) therefore assumes greater importance as an alternate resource in the current scenario of increasing demand and diminishing supplies especially for those countries without any REE resources of their own.

The recovery of REEs from waste resources has been mainly focussed on recycling production scrap, end-of-life products and left-over residues during the production of REEs or REE based electronics and other products. End-of-life products being recycled for REEs can be organised into several distinct categories depending on the nature of the product, REEs present and the availability of recyclable material (Tunsu et al., 2015). Phosphor based products such as CRT screens, Plasma display panels, LEDs, fluorescent lamps are a good source of Y and Eu, and contain small amounts of La, Ce, Tb, Gd, Nd and Sm etc., and some metals as well (Buchert et al., 2012; Ronda et al., 1998). Another category is based on products containing permanent NdFeB magnets such as hard disc drives (HDDs), electric motors, generators for wind turbines, mobile phones, speakers, head-phones, NMR spectrometers etc. REEs present in these magnets include Nd, Dy, Pr, Gd, Tb and Sm along with metals such as copper, nickel, iron, cobalt etc. (Gutfleich et al., 2011). Another category is rechargeable batteries for domestic applications, portable electronic devices, hybrid electric cars, power tools. NiMH batteries, with significant technological and environmental advantages, have replaced Cd in NiCd batteries with a mixed alloy containing La, Pr, Ce and Nd (up to 7% REEs) (Fernendes et al., 2013). Rare earth catalysts including styrene catalysts, fluid cracking and automobile converter catalysts present yet another category, containing mainly La, Ce, Pr, Sm etc. (Feron and Henry, 2015). Small amounts of REEs may also be present in numerous other components used in a range of applications.

Several of the REE recycling techniques such as physical, hydrometallurgical and pyrometallurgical processing, liquid metal extraction, chemical vapor transport, magnetic separation, hydrogen decrepitation etc. were developed for relatively homogeneous and clean pre-consumer magnetic scrap (Itoh et al., 2009; Zakotnik et al., 2008; Saito et al., 2003, Tunsu et al., 2015). Only a few studies have been reported on the recovery of REEs from heterogenous waste from end-of-life products. Abrahami et al. (2015) have reported on the recycling of hard-disc drives (HDDs) and NdFeB magnets using commercial shredding, thermal demagnetisation, grinding and screening followed by molten slag extraction or by acidic leaching. Recovered products were in the form of high purity rare earth double salt NaNd(SO ) for further processing. Using selective chlorination, Xu and Peng (2009) added aluminium chloride to SmCo manufacturing scrap to recover high purity chlorides of Sm and cobalt. Based on hydrogen decrepitation for breaking RE alloys into powders, Pearson (2013) has developed a recycling technique to extract rare metals from NdFeB and SmCo magnets. Several large manufacturing companies are making serious and concerted efforts towards recycling rechargeable batteries; the Umicore battery recycling division can process up to 7000 tonnes of batteries per annum (Umicore battery recycling, 2015). Some of these technologies for recovering REEs from permanent magnets, phosphors and batteries have reached a level of maturity for commercial utilization.

The volumes of e-waste are continuing to grow rapidly in most countries with no signs of slowing down due to rapid upgrades, technological changes, increasing affordability, product obsolescence and escalating consumption of electronic goods. Approximately 44.7 million tonnes of e-waste were generated globally in 2016, and estimated to increase to 55.2 million tonnes by 2021 (Baldé et al., 2017). In view of volumes generated, composition, costs and environmental impacts associated with mining, e-waste is considered a valuable urban mining resource for materials (Hagelüken, 2010). E-waste constitutes a complex inventory of product categories that are assembled out of a variety of components, multiple sub-assemblies and material combinations.

Most of the material recovery from waste PCBs has been focussed on recovering precious and other metals (Cayumil et al., 2016; Cui and Zhang, 2008). The recovery of REEs from waste electronics has been limited to separating magnetic components, batteries, CRTs, screens etc. from the end-of-life equipment for further processing. However, very little attention has been paid to extracting REEs from waste printed circuit boards (PCBs), the central component of electronic devices. The extraction of relatively small amounts of various REEs present in various electronic components mounted on PCBs was generally considered to be economically unviable.

In this article, we have focussed our attention on extracting REEs from a variety of waste PCBs, in addition to other metals, with an aim to produce a concentrated REE resource in a cost-effective and environmentally sustainable manner. The aim of the present investigation is to recover REEs from waste PCBs as concentrated recyclates for further processing, while enhancing the process efficiency, economic and the environmental sustainability by maximizing overall amounts of materials recovered during the recycling of waste PCBs. The article is organised as follows. Experimental details on processing four different types of PCBs, their initial processing, heat treatments in resistance and plasma furnaces, and the generation of pyrolysis residues are presented in Section 2. Section 3 presents inductively coupled plasma (ICP) results on the concentrations of REEs recovered from various pyrolysis fractions; recovery results on precious and other metals will not be presented. In Section 4, these results are discussed in terms of type of PCB, processing conditions, recovery of light and heavy REEs. Key findings of this study will be presented in concluding remarks.

## 2. Materials and methods

## 2.1. Materials

Waste printed circuit boards were collected from a range of sources, waste dismantlers/e-waste recyclers in as received sizes and shapes (see Fig. 1 for representative examples of waste PCBs). These PCBs were labelled as: mobile phones: (MB); mother board: (MTB); power supply: (PS); random access memory: (RAM) in the text as well as in the figures. Electronic components mounted on these boards were left intact and were not removed from the boards for two key reasons. Firstly, REEs have a higher probability of presence within some of the electronic components such as capacitors, integrated circuits, resistors, transistors, LEDs, switches than on the copper laminated substrates. Secondly, the removal of components from PCBs by melting solders with infrared heaters, hot fluids, mechanically breaking solder joints with hammers or grinders, chemical etching etc. is associated with local area contamination, health and environmental risks (Lee et al., 2012). Apart from cutting larger boards into smaller pieces depending on the size and volume of the furnace used for heat treatments, no other mechanical treatment (hammering, crushing, grinding, or powdering) was carried out on these PCBs.

## 2.2. High temperature pyrolysis

The heat treatment of waste PCBs was carried out in two different types of furnaces: (a) a horizontal resistance furnace, (b) a thermal plasma furnace. The plasma furnace generates a high level of turbulence in the heating zone, whereas only turbulence in the horizontal furnace was caused by the continuous flow of inert gas (1 L/min). Heat treatment temperatures were chosen to be approximately850 ^∘C as the generation of harmful dioxins/furans generated from waste PCBs becomes negligibly small at temperatures above 700 C (Saini et al., 2017). Higher temperatures (above the melting point of copper: 1085 C) were not considered necessary based on our previous experience on the recovery of copper from waste PCBs, as these led to enhanced mixing and the formation of mixed alloys (Cayumil et al., 2014). Operational details of the two furnaces are provided next.

A schematic representation of the horizontal resistance furnace is given in Fig. 2a. Basic characteristics of this furnace were as follows: furnace length: 1200 mm; heating zone: 630 mm long, 54 mm diameter, 3 mm wall thickness; heating rate: up to 40 C/min, sample weight: up to 0.02 kg; Gas flow: Ar gas at 1 L/min. Waste PCB pieces were placed on the sample holder and the furnace was heated to 850 C, held at that temperature for 15 min (up to 60 min in some cases), and then furnace cooled. Pyrolysis residues were collected for further characterization.

A schematic representation of the thermal plasma furnace shown in Fig. 2b. This pot type 35 kW DC extended transfer arc plasma reactor uses zircon coated graphite crucible as the furnace hearth. DC transferred arc plasma was used to create high energy density/temperatures between the two graphite electrodes arranged in a vertical configuration (Gomez et al., 2009). Size reduced PCBs were placed in the graphite crucible of the plasma reactor. The plasma furnace was operated using 100 A current and a DC voltage of 50 V. Argon gas was passed continuously through the furnace at a flow rate of 1 L/min with typical heating rates 750 C/min. The reactor was closed at the top with a graphite lid and was thermally insulated. The assembly of the graphite crucible and the bottom electrode together (the ‘anode’), was kept stationary during the furnace operation. The formation and the stabilization of the extended arc plasma were carried out by the movement of the top electrode (the ‘cathode’) using a rack and pinion mechanism. An arc was created by the electrical breakdown of gases; extreme heat generated stripped electrons from gas molecules resulting in an ionized gas or plasma. A water cooling system at the end of two electrodes was used to prevent excessive heating.

Waste PCBs were heat treated at 850 ^∘C for 15 min, and the pyrolysis residues were collected after the furnace had cooled down. While the gas flow rates were maintained at 1L/min for both furnaces, the heating rates were significantly different due to differences in furnace operations.

## 2.3. Characterization of pyrolysis residues

The weights of waste PCBs were recorded before and after the heat treatment. PCBs boards had separated in to copper rich red fraction, tin and lead rich whitish metallic fraction and a dark carbonaceous ceramic phase (see Fig. 3 for representative examples of these fractions) in both furnaces. The weight loss and yield of various fractions following pyrolysis in the horizontal resistance and plasma furnaces is presented in Tables 1 and 2 respectively. Not much difference (except for MBs) was observed in the pyrolysis yields from the two furnaces. Experiments were repeated at least three times for all PCBs in both furnaces to enhance the reproducibility of results, and to compensate for the initial variability in raw waste specimens to some extent. The deviation in the results was found to be within ±5%. The chemical composition of these solid products was then determined using Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectrometers model Perkin Elmer Optima 7300DV ICP-OES. Although the concentrations of major, minor, and precious metals were determined, we have focussed our attention on the recovery of REEs in various fractions in this paper.

## 3. Results

Results from different types of PCBs (MB, MTB, PS and RAM) have been presented in Figs. 4–7 as clustered set of three columns.

The first column in these figures indicates REE concentration in the copper-rich red metallic fraction, the second column for the tin/lead rich white metallic fraction, and the third column for the slag rich carbonaceous residue. REEs recovered from the high temperature pyrolysis of waste PCBs were separated in two distinct groups: Light Rare Earth Elements (LREE) and Heavy Rare Earth Elements (HREE) (Gschneider, 1966). Following elements (also known as the Cerium Group) were classified in the LREE

group: La, Ce, Pr, Nd, Sm, Eu and Gd; the elements in the HREE group included: Tb, Dy and Y. HREEs are less abundant than the LREEs and are thus of higher value. Some HREEs are listed as critical as the use of these elements is presently outstripping supply.

## 3.1. Recovery of REEs from the horizontal resistance furnace

Results for LREEs recovered from four PCBs after heat treatment (850 C; 15 min) in the horizontal resistance furnace are presented in Fig. 4. The data for La, Nd, Gd, Pr, Sm and Ce has been presented; the concentration of rest of the LREEs was found to be negligibly small for an accurate measurement. The concentration of all these REEs was found to be negligibly small in the red and white metallic fractions for all PCBs under investigation. Most of the REEs were found concentrated in the carbonaceous phase. There was a wide variation in the concentrations of REEs recovered across different PCBs. These were found to occur in the following ranges: La (2– 15 ppm); Nd (33–81 ppm); Gd (4–73 ppm); Pr (3–5 ppm); Sm (0.2–0.9 ppm); Ce (3–22 ppm). No specific order could be observed between various PCBs: highest amounts of Nd (81 ppm) were recovered from mother boards and highest amounts of Gd (73 ppm) were recovered from mobile phones.

The results for the HREEs, Dy and Y are presented in Fig. 5. The presence of other HREEs could not be detected. Once again, these two elements were found concentrated in the carbonaceous residue with negligible levels recorded for red and white metallic fractions. There was a wide variation across different PCBs with the levels of Dy ranging between 1 and 60 ppm, and Y ranging between 5 and 22 ppm. The highest amount of 60 ppm of Dy was recovered from mobile phones, and the highest amount of 22 ppm of Y was recovered from mother boards.

## 3.2. Recovery of REEs from the thermal plasma furnace

Results for LREEs recovered from four PCBs after heat treatment (850 C; 15 min) in the thermal plasma furnace are presented in Fig. 6. The data for La, Nd, Gd, Pr, Sm and Ce has been presented; the concentration of rest of the LREEs was once again found to be negligibly small. After heat treatment in the thermal plasma furnace, the concentration of all these REEs was negligibly small in the red and white metallic fractions for all PCBs under investigation. Most of the REEs were found concentrated in the carbonaceous phase. This result is in good agreement with the results from the horizontal resistance furnace. However, there was a significant increase in the levels of REE recovered. The concentrations of REEs recovery across different PCBs were as follows: La (60–361 ppm); Nd (13–821 ppm); Gd (14–75 ppm); Pr (2–100 ppm); Sm (2–55 ppm); Ce (8–20 ppm). Highest amounts of all six REEs, i.e., La (361 ppm), Nd (821 ppm), Gd (75 ppm), Pr (100 ppm), Sm (55 ppm) and Ce (20 ppm) were recovered from power supply boards. The recovery of REEs was generally small from mother boards as well as from RAMs.

The results HREEs Dy and Y after heat treatment in the thermal plasma furnace are presented in Fig. 7; the presence of other HREEs could not be detected. Once again, most of these elements were found concentrated in the carbonaceous residue with negligible levels recorded for the both metallic fractions. The levels of Dy and Y were found to range between 0 and 75 ppm, and between 4 and 57 ppm respectively. While good recovery of these HREEs was recorded from mobile phones, mother boards and power supplies, there was negligible recovery of these elements from RAM boards.

## 4. Discussion

Results on REE recovery from waste PCBs under investigation showed some interesting and novel characteristics. These will be discussed next along with implications for enhancing material recovery and economic sustainability of recycling electronic waste.

## 4.1. Concentration of REEs in the carbonaceous phase

One of the key features of the recovery of REEs from waste PCBs (Figs. 4–7) was the near complete absence of rare earths in the copper rich and lead/tin rich metallic fractions. This was observed for all PCBs under investigation, for the resistance as well as the plasma furnace, and for all eight REEs (LREEs as well as HREEs) recovered. This is an important result that shows most of the REEs that could be extracted from waste PCBs were present in the carbonaceous residue. Given that most e-waste recycling approaches had generally focussed on recovering precious metals, copper and other minor metals, slag rich carbonaceous residue was generally considered a waste biproduct of recycling. We had previously shown the formation of novel carbon fibres and foams during recycling of waste PCBs at high temperatures (1250–1550 C) (Khanna et al., 2015), but also had not paid much attention to the presence of REEs. Key constituents of the carbonaceous phase were refractory oxides silica, alumina, carbon and some residual metals (Khanna et al., 2015). Our results therefore indicate a generally high affinity of various REEs for refractory oxides and/or carbon, and marginal affinities with copper or minor metals present in e-waste. Due to small amounts of REEs recovered, their chemical compositions and diverse nature, it is not possible to make specific comments about individual REEs based on these results. With most the REEs concentrated within the carbonaceous residue, this waste product has the potential to be a valuable material resource and enhance the overall economics and viability of recycling e-waste.

## 4.2. The influence of turbulence on REE recovery

Due to variations in the compositions, functionality and components mounted on various PCBs, some differences in the recovery of REEs are to be expected. As various PCBs present in commercial e-waste are likely to be all mixed up and rarely segregated, averages were computed for REE recoveries from four PCBs under investigation. These averages are expected to represent typical material recoveries at commercial e-waste recycling facilities. Average recoveries of various REEs from the horizontal resistance furnace (‘black columns’) and from the thermal plasma furnace (‘spotted columns’) are shown in Fig. 8. These results are from the slag rich carbonaceous residue only. The REE recoveries from pyrolysis in the thermal plasma furnace was found to be consistently higher than the corresponding recoveries in the horizontal furnace. Scale factors (Plasma: Resistance heating) for various REEs were divided in two categories. High scale factors were observed for La (11:1); Pr (17:2); Sm (25:1) and Y (37:11); and moderate scale factors were observed for Nd (19:13); Gd (17:12); Ce (13:11) and Dy (2:1). These results show that turbulence in the furnace played an important role in dislodging/or dissociating REEs from their host systems and their subsequent recovery in pyrolysis residues. Based on these scale factors, it appears that La, Pr, Sm and Y were tightly bound in electronic components/PCBs and required turbulent conditions for their release, whereas Nd, Gd, Ce and Dy found it relatively easy to dissociate and getting released from the waste. These results show that turbulent conditions during pyrolysis (plasma or even induction furnace) were generally beneficial for enhancing the recovery of REEs from waste PCBs.

## 4.3. Waste PCBs as an urban mining resource of REEs

Results presented above have clearly shown that significant amounts of REEs could be recovered as concentrated recyclates for further processing and extraction of individual rare earths. This resource has been ignored so far with attention mainly focussed on processing highly concentrated REE resources such as magnets, batteries or phosphors. Waste PCBs are already being processed with a variety of techniques for recovering copper, precious metals gold, silver and platinum, and minor metals as well. The recovery of REEs in addition to these materials, will have a positive impact on the economics of the process by enhancing the profitability of recycling electronic waste at no additional cost. Further beneficiation, separation and extraction of individual REEs from these waste concentrates is beyond the scope of this study. Additional details on the recovery of REEs from mineral resources, processing and separation techniques can be found elsewhere (See Gupta and Krishnamurthy, 2005; Jordens et al., 2013; Akcil et al., 2017).

Waste PCBs could therefore be used as a valuable urban mining resource for a whole range of REEs. Given the current supply situation of REEs, increasing demands, China’ monopoly and difficulties faced by countries without their own REE resources, the recovery of REEs from waste PCBs could play an important role in relieving the pressure on global REE supplies to some extent. While recycling cannot replace virgin mining and the production of REEs from natural deposits, urban mining can provide an additional resource to supplement extractions from geologica deposits and prevent excessive mining. The composition of REE concentrates are also expected to be much less complex. Waste PCBs will be a very valuable REE resource for countries with no or little REE natural deposits.

## 5. Concluding remarks

In-depth investigations were carried out on the recovery of wide range of REEs from waste PCBs using resistance as well as thermal plasma furnaces. Key findings of this investigation are summarized below:

1. Waste PCBs were found to be a valuable resource of REEs. Light REEs recovered included La, Nd, Gd, Pr, Sm and Ce, heavy REEs Dy and Y. Three of the REEs recovered, i.e., Nd, Dy and Y were from among the list of most critical material resources.

2. Most of the REEs were found concentrated in the slag rich carbonaceous fraction with negligible levels detected in the copper rich as well as in the tin/lead rich metallic fractions. This result was observed for all PCBs under investigation and for both types of furnaces.

3. A wide variation was observed in the concentrations of REEs recovered from PCBs under investigation. There were no specific correlations between the level of REEs recovered and the type of PCB. The REE recovery was generally poor from RAM boards as compared to the corresponding recoveries mobiles, mother boards and power supply boards.

4. Turbulence was found to play an important role in enhancing the yield from waste PCBs. Much higher levels of REEs were recovered after pyrolysis in the thermal plasma furnace, with inherently high turbulence levels within the furnace. The recoveries were much smaller after pyrolysis in the resistance furnace with little local turbulence. By using plasma furnace, REE recovery yields showed increases ranging from 118% to 2500% for various elements.

5. With the recoveries of a wide variety of REEs from waste PCBs, this study has shown that pyrolysis residues (slag rich carbonaceous phase) from waste PCBs have the potential to become a valuable urban mining resource for REEs, especially for those economies with little or no REE resources of their own.

6. By recovering REEs in addition to precious and other metals from waste PCBs, this novel study has helped enhance the economic viability and profitability of recycling electronic waste. These findings are expected to play an important role in making recycling a key player in the management of burgeoning volumes of electronic waste, and towards sustainable developments in the field.

records.section_name: 1. Introduction Rare earth elements (REEs) are playing an increasingly crucial and vital role in the electronics industry in applications such as Plasma screens, LEDs, Cathode-ray tubes (CRTs), permanent NdFeB magnets, mobile phones, computers and peripherals, motors, wind turbines, rechargeable batteries etc. (Binnemans et al., 2013). Several REEs, such as Neodymium (Nd), Praseodymium (Pr), Gadolinium (Gd), Dysprosium (Dy), Terbium (Tb), Lanthanum (La), Cerium (Ce), Europium (Eu), Terbium (Tb), Yttrium (Y), are essential to the manufacture of several electronic components. These components include permanent magnets (Nd, Pr, Gd, Dy and Tb); rechargeable batteries (La, Ce, Nd and Pr), phosphors (Eu, Tb, Y, Ce, Gd, La), plasma screens (Eu, Tb, Y, Ce, La), auto catalysts (Dy, Nd, Pr, Tb) and other applications (Curtis, 2010). Due to increasing demand, high prices, restricted supplies and monopoly issues, U.S. Department of Energy (2011) has identified five REEs, i.e., Nd, Eu, Tb, Dy and Y, as most critical resources in terms of medium-term criticality index. Over the next 25 years, the demand for Nd and Dy is expected to rise by 700% and 2600% respectively for applications in green, low-carbon economies and other potential sectors (Alonso et al., 2012). Rare earth elements are not exactly rare in nature; these can be found in more than 200 minerals (British Geological Survey, 2011). However, key difficulties in their mining are caused by low concentrations in poor grade ores for economic and sustainable mining, the production of radioactive thorium as a biproduct, regulatory pressures etc. (Kara et al., 2010). With China presently supplying over 90% of the market share of REEs, creating a near monopoly situation, the availability of REEs to enterprises outside China can be potentially challenging, limited by export quotas, expensive, crucial and even a political issue (Moss et al., 2013; Hoenderdaal et al., 2013). Other countries that produce REEs include Australia, USA, India, Brazil, Malaysia etc. In view of emerging new technologies based on REEs and the present supply situation, efforts are being made for further exploration, mining, and enhancing process efficiency of various process steps. Recycling of REEs (presently < 1%) therefore assumes greater importance as an alternate resource in the current scenario of increasing demand and diminishing supplies especially for those countries without any REE resources of their own. The recovery of REEs from waste resources has been mainly focussed on recycling production scrap, end-of-life products and left-over residues during the production of REEs or REE based electronics and other products. End-of-life products being recycled for REEs can be organised into several distinct categories depending on the nature of the product, REEs present and the availability of recyclable material (Tunsu et al., 2015). Phosphor based products such as CRT screens, Plasma display panels, LEDs, fluorescent lamps are a good source of Y and Eu, and contain small amounts of La, Ce, Tb, Gd, Nd and Sm etc., and some metals as well (Buchert et al., 2012; Ronda et al., 1998). Another category is based on products containing permanent NdFeB magnets such as hard disc drives (HDDs), electric motors, generators for wind turbines, mobile phones, speakers, head-phones, NMR spectrometers etc.

records.section_name: 1. Introduction Rare earth elements (REEs) are playing an increasingly crucial and vital role in the electronics industry in applications such as Plasma screens, LEDs, Cathode-ray tubes (CRTs), permanent NdFeB magnets, mobile phones, computers and peripherals, motors, wind turbines, rechargeable batteries etc. (Binnemans et al., 2013). Several REEs, such as Neodymium (Nd), Praseodymium (Pr), Gadolinium (Gd), Dysprosium (Dy), Terbium (Tb), Lanthanum (La), Cerium (Ce), Europium (Eu), Terbium (Tb), Yttrium (Y), are essential to the manufacture of several electronic components. These components include permanent magnets (Nd, Pr, Gd, Dy and Tb); rechargeable batteries (La, Ce, Nd and Pr), phosphors (Eu, Tb, Y, Ce, Gd, La), plasma screens (Eu, Tb, Y, Ce, La), auto catalysts (Dy, Nd, Pr, Tb) and other applications (Curtis, 2010). Due to increasing demand, high prices, restricted supplies and monopoly issues, U.S. Department of Energy (2011) has identified five REEs, i.e., Nd, Eu, Tb, Dy and Y, as most critical resources in terms of medium-term criticality index. Over the next 25 years, the demand for Nd and Dy is expected to rise by 700% and 2600% respectively for applications in green, low-carbon economies and other potential sectors (Alonso et al., 2012). Rare earth elements are not exactly rare in nature; these can be found in more than 200 minerals (British Geological Survey, 2011). However, key difficulties in their mining are caused by low concentrations in poor grade ores for economic and sustainable mining, the production of radioactive thorium as a biproduct, regulatory pressures etc. (Kara et al., 2010). With China presently supplying over 90% of the market share of REEs, creating a near monopoly situation, the availability of REEs to enterprises outside China can be potentially challenging, limited by export quotas, expensive, crucial and even a political issue (Moss et al., 2013; Hoenderdaal et al., 2013). Other countries that produce REEs include Australia, USA, India, Brazil, Malaysia etc. In view of emerging new technologies based on REEs and the present supply situation, efforts are being made for further exploration, mining, and enhancing process efficiency of various process steps. Recycling of REEs (presently < 1%) therefore assumes greater importance as an alternate resource in the current scenario of increasing demand and diminishing supplies especially for those countries without any REE resources of their own. The recovery of REEs from waste resources has been mainly focussed on recycling production scrap, end-of-life products and left-over residues during the production of REEs or REE based electronics and other products. End-of-life products being recycled for REEs can be organised into several distinct categories depending on the nature of the product, REEs present and the availability of recyclable material (Tunsu et al., 2015). Phosphor based products such as CRT screens, Plasma display panels, LEDs, fluorescent lamps are a good source of Y and Eu, and contain small amounts of La, Ce, Tb, Gd, Nd and Sm etc., and some metals as well (Buchert et al., 2012; Ronda et al., 1998). Another category is based on products containing permanent NdFeB magnets such as hard disc drives (HDDs), electric motors, generators for wind turbines, mobile phones, speakers, head-phones, NMR spectrometers etc.

text_chunk.text:
## 2.2. High temperature pyrolysis
The heat treatment of waste PCBs was carried out in two different types of furnaces: (a) a horizontal resistance furnace, (b) a thermal plasma furnace. The plasma furnace generates a high level of turbulence in the heating zone, whereas only turbulence in the horizontal furnace was caused by the continuous flow of inert gas (1 L/min). Heat treatment temperatures were chosen to be approximately850 ^∘C as the generation of harmful dioxins/furans generated from waste PCBs becomes negligibly small at temperatures above 700 C (Saini et al., 2017). Higher temperatures (above the melting point of copper: 1085 C) were not considered necessary based on our previous experience on the recovery of copper from waste PCBs, as these led to enhanced mixing and the formation of mixed alloys (Cayumil et al., 2014). Operational details of the two furnaces are provided next.
A schematic representation of the horizontal resistance furnace is given in Fig. 2a. Basic characteristics of this furnace were as follows: furnace length: 1200 mm; heating zone: 630 mm long, 54 mm diameter, 3 mm wall thickness; heating rate: up to 40 C/min, sample weight: up to 0.02 kg; Gas flow: Ar gas at 1 L/min. Waste PCB pieces were placed on the sample holder and the furnace was heated to 850 C, held at that temperature for 15 min (up to 60 min in some cases), and then furnace cooled. Pyrolysis residues were collected for further characterization.
A schematic representation of the thermal plasma furnace shown in Fig. 2b. This pot type 35 kW DC extended transfer arc plasma reactor uses zircon coated graphite crucible as the furnace hearth. DC transferred arc plasma was used to create high energy density/temperatures between the two graphite electrodes arranged in a vertical configuration (Gomez et al., 2009). Size reduced PCBs were placed in the graphite crucible of the plasma reactor. The plasma furnace was operated using 100 A current and a DC voltage of 50 V. Argon gas was passed continuously through the furnace at a flow rate of 1 L/min with typical heating rates 750 C/min. The reactor was closed at the top with a graphite lid and was thermally insulated. The assembly of the graphite crucible and the bottom electrode together (the ‘anode’), was kept stationary during the furnace operation. The formation and the stabilization of the extended arc plasma were carried out by the movement of the top electrode (the ‘cathode’) using a rack and pinion mechanism. An arc was created by the electrical breakdown of gases; extreme heat generated stripped electrons from gas molecules resulting in an ionized gas or plasma. A water cooling system at the end of two electrodes was used to prevent excessive heating.
Waste PCBs were heat treated at 850 ^∘C for 15 min, and the pyrolysis residues were collected after the furnace had cooled down. While the gas flow rates were maintained at 1L/min for both furnaces, the heating rates were significantly different due to differences in furnace operations.

text_chunk.text:
## 3.1. Recovery of REEs from the horizontal resistance furnace
Results for LREEs recovered from four PCBs after heat treatment (850 C; 15 min) in the horizontal resistance furnace are presented in Fig. 4. The data for La, Nd, Gd, Pr, Sm and Ce has been presented; the concentration of rest of the LREEs was found to be negligibly small for an accurate measurement. The concentration of all these REEs was found to be negligibly small in the red and white metallic fractions for all PCBs under investigation. Most of the REEs were found concentrated in the carbonaceous phase. There was a wide variation in the concentrations of REEs recovered across different PCBs. These were found to occur in the following ranges: La (2– 15 ppm); Nd (33–81 ppm); Gd (4–73 ppm); Pr (3–5 ppm); Sm (0.2–0.9 ppm); Ce (3–22 ppm). No specific order could be observed between various PCBs: highest amounts of Nd (81 ppm) were recovered from mother boards and highest amounts of Gd (73 ppm) were recovered from mobile phones.
The results for the HREEs, Dy and Y are presented in Fig. 5. The presence of other HREEs could not be detected. Once again, these two elements were found concentrated in the carbonaceous residue with negligible levels recorded for red and white metallic fractions. There was a wide variation across different PCBs with the levels of Dy ranging between 1 and 60 ppm, and Y ranging between 5 and 22 ppm. The highest amount of 60 ppm of Dy was recovered from mobile phones, and the highest amount of 22 ppm of Y was recovered from mother boards.

text_chunk.text:
## 3.2. Recovery of REEs from the thermal plasma furnace
Results for LREEs recovered from four PCBs after heat treatment (850 C; 15 min) in the thermal plasma furnace are presented in Fig. 6. The data for La, Nd, Gd, Pr, Sm and Ce has been presented; the concentration of rest of the LREEs was once again found to be negligibly small. After heat treatment in the thermal plasma furnace, the concentration of all these REEs was negligibly small in the red and white metallic fractions for all PCBs under investigation. Most of the REEs were found concentrated in the carbonaceous phase. This result is in good agreement with the results from the horizontal resistance furnace. However, there was a significant increase in the levels of REE recovered. The concentrations of REEs recovery across different PCBs were as follows: La (60–361 ppm); Nd (13–821 ppm); Gd (14–75 ppm); Pr (2–100 ppm); Sm (2–55 ppm); Ce (8–20 ppm). Highest amounts of all six REEs, i.e., La (361 ppm), Nd (821 ppm), Gd (75 ppm), Pr (100 ppm), Sm (55 ppm) and Ce (20 ppm) were recovered from power supply boards. The recovery of REEs was generally small from mother boards as well as from RAMs.
The results HREEs Dy and Y after heat treatment in the thermal plasma furnace are presented in Fig. 7; the presence of other HREEs could not be detected. Once again, most of these elements were found concentrated in the carbonaceous residue with negligible levels recorded for the both metallic fractions. The levels of Dy and Y were found to range between 0 and 75 ppm, and between 4 and 57 ppm respectively. While good recovery of these HREEs was recorded from mobile phones, mother boards and power supplies, there was negligible recovery of these elements from RAM boards.

text_chunk.text:
## 5. Concluding remarks
In-depth investigations were carried out on the recovery of wide range of REEs from waste PCBs using resistance as well as thermal plasma furnaces. Key findings of this investigation are summarized below:
1. Waste PCBs were found to be a valuable resource of REEs. Light REEs recovered included La, Nd, Gd, Pr, Sm and Ce, heavy REEs Dy and Y. Three of the REEs recovered, i.e., Nd, Dy and Y were from among the list of most critical material resources.
2. Most of the REEs were found concentrated in the slag rich carbonaceous fraction with negligible levels detected in the copper rich as well as in the tin/lead rich metallic fractions. This result was observed for all PCBs under investigation and for both types of furnaces.
3. A wide variation was observed in the concentrations of REEs recovered from PCBs under investigation. There were no specific correlations between the level of REEs recovered and the type of PCB. The REE recovery was generally poor from RAM boards as compared to the corresponding recoveries mobiles, mother boards and power supply boards.
4. Turbulence was found to play an important role in enhancing the yield from waste PCBs. Much higher levels of REEs were recovered after pyrolysis in the thermal plasma furnace, with inherently high turbulence levels within the furnace. The recoveries were much smaller after pyrolysis in the resistance furnace with little local turbulence. By using plasma furnace, REE recovery yields showed increases ranging from 118% to 2500% for various elements.
5. With the recoveries of a wide variety of REEs from waste PCBs, this study has shown that pyrolysis residues (slag rich carbonaceous phase) from waste PCBs have the potential to become a valuable urban mining resource for REEs, especially for those economies with little or no REE resources of their own.
6. By recovering REEs in addition to precious and other metals from waste PCBs, this novel study has helped enhance the economic viability and profitability of recycling electronic waste. These findings are expected to play an important role in making recycling a key player in the management of burgeoning volumes of electronic waste, and towards sustainable developments in the field.
